1. Summary

General context

Iris is a higher-order separation logic [1] used to verify properties about programs. Its flexible notion of resources allows it to be applied to a variety of projects such as a foundational verification tool for C [2], a semantic model for Rust types [3], and a separation logic to reason about probabilistic programs [4], among others. The main way to use the Iris logic is through its formalization in the Rocq proof assistant. Beyond an encoding of its logic, the formalization also provides a set of custom tactics and associated abstractions to interact with the Iris logic [5]. The Iris Proof Mode is not unique to the Iris logic, but instead works over an abstract notion of separation logic. This principle of working over abstract definitions to enforce boundaries between different parts of the system is characteristic of the Iris project.

To support this amount of extensibility, the Iris development is constantly confronted by the constraints of their chosen system of mechanization. In response, the Iris project has had to either compromise or develop new innovative ways to use the tools at their disposal. This makes Iris a particularly interesting case study when comparing different systems of mechanization. When Lean, a new proof assistant offering a flexible metaprogramming API and advanced automation tools, started gaining popularity amongst the programming languages community, some contributors of the Iris project started wondering how an alternate formalization of Iris in Lean would look.

Arguably, the reason why Lean is able to offer a greater deal of flexibility comes from the fact that Lean is implemented in Lean itself. This bootstrapping setup has made it so it is straightforward to expose a powerful metaprogramming API by simply giving its users access to the same features used in the internal development of Lean.

Research problem

It is not yet clear how much an Iris formalization could benefit from Lean’s features. The Iris project has grown organically to adapt to the constraints and features of Rocq, which differ from those in Lean. In particular, the Iris project relies heavily on some features of Rocq’s typeclass search which are not available in Lean due to their performance implications. Furthermore, Rocq’s kernel supports features Lean’s kernel does not, the most salient example being coinductive types. Despite Lean recently landing support for coinductive predicates, codata is not natively supported by its theory. For the Iris project this is relevant because there has recently been an effort to develop a unified program logic based on interaction trees [6], which require this feature.

On the other hand, it has not been explored how Lean could enable more advanced automation tools for Iris. One big obstacle in this endeavour is the fact that, at the start of my internship, the Iris Lean development was not advanced enough to make a connection between the Iris logic and program semantics. This made it impossible to consider the advantages of new or existing automation, since there were no case studies to apply them to.

Contributions

We explore the impacts of a Lean mechanization of the Iris logic in two ways.

On the one hand, we study how to best deal with new constraints imposed by the switch. We focus in particular on the encoding of interaction trees in Lean. There had already been efforts on addressing Lean’s lack of coinductive data types through the QPFTypes [7] library, with most other approaches relying on the same underlying concept. Instead, we choose to focus on exploring a different encoding that had been used in Lean’s standard library to define streams, the Std.Iter API. Based on the underlying ideas, we develop an encoding1 of interaction trees and use them to define a variety of programs. We also provide a definition of strong and weak bisimulation for this datatype, and report on our attempts to improve the API provided by this encoding. Unfortunately, we have found our studied encoding to be lacking with respect to the previously available approaches in terms of both ease of use, performance and flexibility of its definitions.

On the other hand, we explore the benefits of a stronger metaprogramming support, by developing an automation tactic for Iris Lean named wander2, alluding to the path one takes around the proof search tree. This tactic is inspired by Iris Rocq’s own Diaframe [8] tactic, but in using Lean’s metaprogramming APIs, also develops the foundations of a framework on which other Iris automation tools can build upon. To build and evaluate the aforementioned tactic, we also contribute to the Iris Lean formalization the required missing components and an assortment of program proofs used as case studies.

Arguments supporting our contribution’s validity

For the interaction tree encoding, we provide the monad operations of the itree and define the iteration combinator, in addition to defining the strong and weak bisimulation relations for interaction trees. We use these definitions to define a variety of example interaction trees, and observe that they fall short in both ergonomics and efficiency to other approaches. Finally, we note some of the attempts made to bridge this usability gap, and the obstacles that prevented them from working.

In terms of the wander tactic, we have evaluated it on a set of simple programs, ranging from the verification of various list functions, including Iris Lean’s now characteristic quicksort example, to the behaviour of functions making use of prophecy variables. In all of these the tactic was able to either make partial progress or close automatically. These examples are enough to showcase the usefulness of the tactic, and serve as a benchmark to identify performance bottlenecks and paths to future improvements.

Summary and future work

With regards to Lean missing native support for coinductive data, we explore a state-machine based encoding and compare it with existing approaches. We conclude that the new encoding does not present any advantages over prior encodings. The future of interaction trees in Lean seems to lie in the QPFTypes [7] approach. A combination of this approach and Lean’s partial_fixpoint machinery seems to have found a particular sweet-spot in terms of flexibility and convenience of the definitions. Using this encoding, a formalization of the program logic for interaction trees described in M. Vistrup, M. Sammler, and R. Jung [6] has been developed in the ISTA-PLV/iris-lean repository. It remains unexplored whether interaction trees may benefit from Lean’s quotients by making weak bisimulation its propositional equality.

By applying wander to some examples, the specific areas which bottleneck its performance have been identified. We highlight the hint-search procedure as the main bottleneck in the tactic’s performance. This matches with Diaframe’s experience, which made the decision to implement an optimization on the procedure using Rocq’s Ltac2 language. In the case of wander, we are confident that such a speedup can be achieved by exploiting features of the current tactic architecture such as tactic shared state and custom caches. There is also hope for further improvements by removing the need for binder encoding through a more unified representation, integrating with more advanced Lean automation features and even using Lean’s asynchronous programming APIs to enable parallel proof reconstruction.

2. State machine encodings of interaction trees

Definitions. In this section, we concern ourselves with encodings of interaction trees [9] (itrees) in Lean. An itree is a datastructure that models computations through their observational behaviour. Under the itree interpretation, a computation is nothing but a procedure that may either invoke an effect or produce a value. It may seem that this representation can be encoded as an inductive type, but in doing so we lose the ability to represent a large family of computations: the diverging computations. This condition is what requires itrees to be defined coinductively, as shown in Listing 1.

An itree of the shape ITree.ret v represents the computation which produces the value v. An itree of the shape ITree.vis eff k represents a computation which emits a visible effect. Visible effects are represented by the Effect structure, and consist of two components: the type of the effect itself, and the type of the output of the effect. The continuing computation k may depend on the output of the effect. Finally, the ITree.tau constructor represents computations which emit a silent effect. This is equivalent to using ITree.vis with a distinguished “silent” effect, but it is included in the definition as its own constructor since it is more of an implementation detail. It can also be seen as an equivalent to the constructor of the Delay monad.

Listing 2 shows how to use the above definition to represent various programs. simpleValue and echo showcase how the first two constructors of an ITree are used. loop models the silent diverging computation, and printLoop models the not-so-silent diverging computation. Finally maybeLoop models a computation with one diverging trace and infinite finite traces.

The issue with all the above examples is that this syntax does not currently exist in Lean. The Lean kernel itself does not support coinductive datatypes, so if one wants to reason about an object like the one shown in Listing 1, they need to encode it in some other way.

Quotients of polynomial functors There has been prior work on these kinds of encodings. The most relevant one is that of data types as quotients of polynomial functors [7], which are accessible in Lean 4 through the library QPFTypes. The aims of this library are broader than simply encoding itrees, its objective is to encode arbitrary data types using this approach. However, not all datatypes can be seen as a particular instance of a polynomial functor 𝑃(𝛼)=∑(𝑥:𝐴),𝐵 𝑥→𝛼. To address this issue and enrich their representation power, the library uses quotients.

Quotients are a feature of Lean’s kernel which is not available in Rocq’s. They allow one to “lose precision” in a type’s equality relation, replacing it by some other equivalence relation instead. The standard way in Lean to represent a type equipped with an equivalence relation is through the Setoid α type. A quotient is simply a type which takes a setoid and makes its equivalence relation into the default propositional equality. Listing 3 shows the primitive operations of the Quot type.

While the QPFTypes approach is more general, quotients are not necessary to encode itrees. Polynomial functors and the underlying principle to generate coinductive data from them are enough to encode itrees. There are other libraries which forgo the complexity of the QPFTypes representation and specialize it to representing itrees. mit-plv/lean-itree4 makes use of the polynomial functor definition of Mathlib to derive its encoding, and builds on top of it an API similar to that of Rocq’s itree library. ISTA-PLV/coinductive takes the same approach, but vendoring in all required definitions to eliminate the Mathlib dependency.

Streams as Std.Iter. There have not been many other different approaches for dealing with coinduction in Lean. The only exception we were aware of was the Std.Iter type, which is included in Lean’s standard library, and which encodes Streams in Lean. A Stream is the coinductive analogue to a list, sharing the same constructors but having the property of being potentially infinite. Haskell users may be familiar with this description, as it corresponds with Haskell’s default list type. Lean’s standard library encodes Streams as a state machine, which iterates over some internal state to produce the stream’s values, potentially without end. Listing 4 shows a simplification of this API.

If we compare the definition of Iter in Listing 4 with that of Stream, we observe that the variants of IterStep correspond precisely with the constructors of Stream. In fact, we can associate Iter.step with doing case analysis on a value of type Stream, where we confuse the internal state of the iterator with the datatype of the Stream.

The Std.Iter definition in Lean’s standard library is particularly nice in that it is efficient to run. This performance is unlocked through compiler optimizations, which themselves rely on the fact that the type of the internal state α in Std.Iter is exposed in its signature. The compiler uses this information to merge consecutive invocations of an iterator’s step function, removing the associated overhead through stream fusion [10]. We observed that the encoding technique used in Listing 4 is not specific to streams, which begged the question: could we use this technique to achieve an encoding for itrees which could inherit some of Std.Iter’s performance properties?

State-machine itree encoding. We consider a definition for itrees inspired by the Std.Iter API, with the following shape.

Using this encoding, we can implement the functions corresponding to the usual itree constructors as shown in Listing 6

The definitions of these constructors are quite complicated. It would be hard to convince users of IterTree to adapt all their definitions to use this encoding instead. Thankfully, when it comes to itrees, it is well known that for most applications, only a couple of combinators are really used. Therefore, it suffices to provide these combinators, and for the most part our users will not have to concern themselves with the underlying details. Beyond the itree constructors these primitives include the monadic bind and iter functions. In Listing 7 we show their signatures, exposing the type of their internal state.

We can now only require our users to encode their functions using the primitives in Listing 6 and Listing 7, which offers a much more convenient API. The only annoyance left is having to quantify over the internal state when receiving an IterTree as a function, but the return type at least can be inferred by the type checker. Unfortunately, this is not the case. Consider the definition of interp_mrec in Listing 8.

The definition above is not valid, since the first two branches of our match determine the type of the resulting internal state to be Unit, while the other branches determine their own, different types for the internal state. This eliminates any hope of having a nice API for this encoding.

To drive the nail in the coffin, this encoding is also not able to benefit from the performance of Std.Iter. The difference has nothing to do with the representation, but with their typical usecases. In fact, the fundamental issue is also present in the Std.Iter API, it is simply not as big of a concern since it is not encountered as often. Consider the following excerpt from the documentation of Std.Iter.append: “This combinator incurs an additional 𝑂(1) cost with each output of it₁ and it₂”. The reason this 𝑂(1) penalty happens is that, when running step, the Std.Iter.append operation must distinguish which iterator is running: the left one or the right one. This penalty is not a big deal for iterators, since they are commonly not composed in this way more than a fixed number of times. However, for itrees this is not the case. As we have seen in Listing 8, it is quite common to want to compose itrees an arbitrary number of times.

The idea behind interp_mrec is that, given a computation producing effects E and D, we produce a function only producing effects E by substituting all effects D using the ctx function. Consider the case of interp_mrec (fun x => .vis (print 1) fun _ => .ret x) printLoop, using the definition of printLoop provided in Listing 2. The resulting itree is equivalent to the silent infinite loop. However, it also produces an unbounded number of itree compositions. If we incur a 𝑂(1) penalty for each composition, we end up with an 𝑂(𝑛) penalty cost at the 𝑛-th step call.

Fixing the usability with quotients. To be able to properly define interp_mrec, we can bundle the type of the internal state inside the IterTree structure, as shown in Listing 9.

This encoding fixes the usability issues, although it does not address the matter of performance. With this definition we were able to define both strong and weak bisimulation as coinductive predicates over the type, and prove they are equivalence relations. We have already mentioned that one can use Quotients in Lean to promote an equivalence relation to propositional equality for its quotient. Therefore, we set out to study, with our encoding, whether it would be possible to hide away the implementation detail of our internal state by making a quotient of the state-machine implementation over the strong bisimulation relation. The issue with this approach came when defining the smart constructor for vis ev k for the quotient. This definition requires that we provide a function which picks a representative IterTree out of the quotient. This can be done by using the quotient itself as the internal state of our state-machine. However, using this implementation incurs a universe bump in our representation which prevents us, among other things, from defining a case analysis principle on our type.

This issue itself can also be sidestepped by using the noncomputable operation Quotient.out, which relies on the axiom of choice to pick a representative. However, at this stage the restrictions for our IterTree definitions became so severe that we decided there was no hope in developing them further. It remains to be seen whether some of these approaches could be useful in other representations.

3. Automation in Iris Lean

In this section, we leave behind the negative result of Section 2 to focus on a more positive result: wander, a Lean tactic to automate Iris goals. First, we must introduce some preliminary definitions. Section 3.1 explains how Iris can be used to prove properties about programs, using an example programming language called HeapLang. Section 3.2 introduces the wander tactic, and showcases how it can be used and extended from a user’s perspective. Section 3.3 goes into the details of wander’s architecture and overall implementation principles. We take a brief detour in Section 3.4 to talk about Lean’s metaprogramming API, and how the Iris Lean project builds on top of it to implement the abstractions of the Iris Proof Mode. Finally, Section 3.5 covers the additional abstractions that were used to build the wander.

3.1. Background: Iris preliminaries

The main purpose of Iris is to serve as a separation logic to verify properties of programs. Iris’ modular design allows one to equip it with a programming language through its operational semantics, and to reason about its behaviour using a weakest precondition transformer 𝐖𝐏𝑒 {Φ}. This predicate states that, if 𝑒 reduces (through the operational semantics) to a value 𝑣, then this value satisfies the property Φ 𝑣. It also admits that 𝑒 diverges, but it rejects the case where 𝑒 gets stuck, that is, where it cannot reduce but is not a value.

Using the weakest precondition transformer, one is able to reason about the features of their programming language by stating how they interact with it. To illustrate this, we consider HeapLang, the example language provided by default in the standard Iris distribution. HeapLang is an ML-like language with additional mutable state and concurrency primitives like 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐤 and 𝐜𝐚𝐬. In Figure 1 we give a definition of its syntax and semantics, in terms of the WP.

Usually, the preferred way to work with program semantics is to use Hoare triples {𝑃} 𝑒 {𝑣,𝑄}. Using the weakest precondition transformer, one can encode Hoare triples as 𝑃−∗𝐖𝐏𝑒 {𝑣,𝑄}. This is not, however, the encoding preferred by Iris. Instead, the Texan triple encoding, given in Figure 2, is used. The reason is that Texan triples are easier to use in proofs, since by generalizing over the shape of the postcondition one removes the need to apply the wand rule.

With the semantics in place, we are now in a position where we can verify properties of programs. To start, let us consider a simple example: a swap function which exchanges the contents of two pointers. Listing 10 shows the definition of the swap function, as well as the Iris proof of its specification, swap_spec.

The proof starts by introducing some hypotheses. In Iris Lean this is done with the iintro tactic. Because of the Texan triple encoding we mentioned before, the first premise introduced is the generalized postcondition Φ. The % preceding the Φ identifier signals to iintro that Φ is to be placed in the regular Lean local context. This is possible for all elements quantified by the ∀, and for pure propositions, denoted by the square corners in ⌜⬚⌝. If an identifier is instead preceded by ∗, the introduced hypothesis is placed in the spatial context of our separation logic instead. This is also the default behaviour if no symbol precedes an identifier (since a hypothesis can always be placed in the spatial context). The proof state to the right in Listing 10 shows the state of both contexts at a particular point in the proof. The hypotheses above the first ⊢ correspond to the pure context. The hypotheses following that, until the next ⊢, correspond to the spatial context. All spatial hypotheses are preceded by ∗.

After introducing these hypotheses, the proof proceeds by applying the 𝐖𝐏 rules shown in Figure 1. This is done through specific tactics, prefixed with a wp_, whose purpose is to provide a convenient syntax for applying these theorems.

The proof concludes by calling iapply. If we observe the proof state of Listing 10, we observe that this corresponds to the continuation in the Texan triple encoding. This is how most proofs of Texan triples finish in general, since the only way to conclude the quantified Φ is by invoking the continuation. What follows is a proof of the stated postcondition 𝑄, which in this case is solved automatically by iframe, a tactic which applies separation logic’s frame rule by matching hypotheses in the spatial context with obligations in the goal. In this proof, this amounts to providing the predicates 𝑥↦𝑣2 and 𝑦↦𝑣1

3.2. wander tutorial

Notice how the proof of Listing 10 was actually quite straightforward. This is not a matter of the function itself being quite simple, which is also true, but that the strategy we followed to close the goal was really simple. If we see something we can introduce, add it to the relevant context. If we see a 𝐖𝐏, apply the relevant rule depending on the expression. If we can obtain the obligation in the goal from a hypothesis, apply that hypothesis. Proceed until the goal is closed.

The strategy behind this proof can be generalized with the name execute the goal. We define an action to take when the goal has some specific shape, and iterate on these actions as much as possible. The key insight is that this strategy is able to make progress on Iris goals often enough that it warrants being automated. This is precisely what Diaframe [8] seeks to do, and wander, being inspired by Diaframe, implements the same strategy. Therefore wander is able to close the swap_spec theorem of Listing 10, as shown in Listing 11.

It is useful to think of wander as, less of a tactic, and more of a custom tactic environment, which can be accessed after the arrow in wander =>. In this environment, we can instruct wander what action to take. The finish action used here instructs wander to perform as many transformations to the goal as possible until the goal is closed, or throw an error otherwise. Because wander applies the strategy mentioned before, it is able to solve this example without a problem.

To illustrate other features of wander we will need a more complicated example. For this purpose, let us define an encoding of integer lists in HeapLang, and prove the specification of a function listInc which increases all the numbers in the list by one.

The listInc example of Listing 12 is more involved, since proofs about its behaviour now need to rely on induction. We can ask wander to perform partial progress by using the continue action, which works like finish except that it will not throw an error if the goal could not be closed, instead it simply returns all goals it couldn’t make progress on. In Listing 13 we show the result of taking this action, along with the first out of the two goals left by wander.

How did we arrive at the above goal? To make progress, wander proceeded by symbolically executing our function as before. When it encountered the match, it did a case analysis on the value l. The first of the remaining goals corresponds to the case where the list we want to increment is empty. However, this information is not present in the goal because wander performed a case-analysis on the value l instead of on the list xs. We can instruct wander how to better perform this case analysis through the use of hints.

Hints are Diaframe’s (and therefore wander’s) mechanism to keep making progress when an unknown proposition is encountered in the goal. wander has support for most of the default connectives in separation logic, but when it finds an unrecognized proposition, it uses it to fetch an appropriate rule it can apply to transform the goal. wander’s rule format is that of Diaframe’s biabduction hints, and it has the following shape.

A biabduction rule like the one in Figure 3 would apply whenever the current goal has the same shape as 𝑇 𝑥 and the spatial context has a hypothesis 𝐻. All other elements of the rule, shown in blue, can be considered as outputs, and are used to transform the goal. In particular, 𝐴 (referred to as the antiframe) becomes a new goal to be solved, and 𝐹 (referred to as the frame) becomes a new spatial premise to consider when solving the rest of the goal. Here are a couple of examples of rules provided by default.

The assumption rule in Listing 14 can be read as “given a goal 𝐴, if 𝐴 can be obtained from the local context, then emp is a new condition to be immediately satisfied, and we obtain resources satisfying emp going forward”. Since in this rule both the antiframe and the frame are trivial, the effect of applying this goal is simply of closing our particular goal. The load_rule rule is a bit more interesting. The frame is still empty, but the antiframe states that to conclude WP hl(!#l) {{ Φ }} one must provide a proof of l ↦ v for some v, and assuming l ↦ v that the postcondition is satisfied for v. This is the rule used to replace wp_load. There are similar rules provided by default for all wp prefixed tactics.

Therefore, it is now clear to see how to proceed with the verification of listInc in Listing 13. It suffices to give wander a hint which instructs it to use the isList predicate to perform a case disjunction upon encountering a match.

Using the rule in Listing 15 and some simplifications (List.map_nil), wander is able to conclude the case of the empty list. However, when making progress on the case where the list has at least one element, we end up in a similar situation again, where we now make a disjunction distinguishing the cases where the list has one element or at least two. The issue is that, to conclude the proof, we don’t need to perform a case disjunction on the list, but reason by induction itself. Implementing a rule which encodes the induction principle is not possible. A general way to allow wander to reason about these kinds of inductive programs is to rely on the fact that Iris is a step-indexed logic and use Löb induction before invoking wander. With the Löb induction principle in the spatial context, wander is able to make progress on the proof automatically, minus some manual simplifications.

3.3. Wander architecture

In Section 3.2 we covered how a user would interact with wander. In this section, we will talk about wander’s architecture, identify its main components, and show how they compare to Diaframe’s.

First and foremost, it’s important to remark that not all Iris goals have a shape that Diaframe, hence wander, can make progress upon. To be precise, Diaframe assumes that its goals do not require introducing hypothesis on left conjuncts, like (∀𝑥,𝑃)∗𝑄. Supporting goals of this shape would require splitting up-front the spatial context between 𝑃 and 𝑄, but Diaframe has no mechanism to deal with this situation. Since wander is based on Diaframe, it inherits this restriction. To be more precise, wander recognizes the following connectives in Iris goals: the structural connectives ⬚∗⬚ and ∃𝑥,⬚, introduction connectives ⬚−∗⬚ and ∀𝑥,⬚, and modalities 𝑀⬚, with a distinguished ▷⬚. The leaves of these connectives are either pure propositions ⌜⬚⌝ or atoms. Additionally, wander may act upon the ∧ connective if it occurs in the top-level position, which is needed to support case analysis. Then, the goals supported by wander are those for which no introduction connective happens on the left-hand side of a separating conjunction.

Goal transformations. The main component behind wander is the goal transformation procedure. This is the part of the tactic which is in charge of constructing the final proof, by inspecting the shape of the current goal and deciding the action to take depending on it. The procedure is really similar with that of Diaframe’s, except for a couple of changes. Here we give a description of wander’s goal transformation algorithm on an input Γ;Δ⊢𝑀𝐺, where Γ is the pure context, Δ is the spatial context, 𝑀 is a modality (or the identity if there is none) and 𝐺 is a goal in the format described above.

The new transformations performed by wander are highlighted in Figure 4 in dark green. These are explicit handling of empty goals, and of a later modality in the left conjunct of a separating conjunction. There are also other differences which cannot be seen in the Figure 4, because they concern transformations which are no longer present in wander. The reason empty goals need to be handled explicitly is because wander only supports biabduction hints, unlike Diaframe which also supports abduction hints. We postpone an explanation of this discrepancy until we talk about the hint search procedure. For all other discrepancies, the explanation lies with the normalizer.

Normalizer. The goal of the normalizer is to transform the goal into a shape the algorithm in Figure 4 can more easily make progress on. The normalizer was originally integrated into wander to address a fundamental discrepancy between how wander and Diaframe distinguish shapes of the goal. Because wander is a metaprogram, it is able to directly match on the expression of the type, and determine syntactically what the shape of the goal is. Diaframe is not implemented with such capabilities, so it relies on typeclasses to perform this matching. The idea is to have a typeclass IntoConnective A B C which establishes that for some input A, there is a proof that A ⊣⊢ conn(B, C). Then, if B and C are outputs of our typeclass, we have established that A has the shape conn(B,C). The benefit of this approach is that the matching does not have to be syntactic. Diaframe tries to keep the matching as simple as possible, but it is not entirely syntactic. In particular, Diaframe is able to deduce that ▷(𝐴∗𝐵) is a separating conjunction over ▷𝐴 and ▷𝐵.

This creates a discrepancy between wander and Diaframe’s procedures. Generally, Diaframe does not need to deal with a ▷ if it happens before a structural connective, since it will just be seen as the structural connective instead. However, wander does not make that distinction by default. To deal with this problem, the normalizer is run before the goal transformations take place, and it makes sure to apply the relevant rewriting theorems to push down appearances of ▷ as far down as possible. This makes it so that we now have to deal with the ▷ in the left hand side of the separating conjunction.

wander’s normalizer is nothing more than an invocation of Lean’s simp simplifier with a curated non-extensible set of rewrite rules stating equivalences between different shapes of goals. Beyond the mimicking of Diaframe’s matching, it quickly became apparent that the normalizer could be exploited to work over more well-behaved goals. What follows are some of these rewrite rules.

However, since the normalizer uses the simp machinery, it is not restricted to applying rewriting rules given by lemmas. In Lean, one is able to define simplification procedures, commonly referred to as simprocs, which use metaprogramming to, given the right-hand side of a rule, compute the left-hand side and the proof that comes with it. This feature is used by wander’s normalizer to implement a Texan triple to Hoare triple conversion.

We have seen in section Section 3.1 that Iris does not use the usual 𝐖𝐏 encoding of Hoare triples. Instead, it uses the Texan triple encoding, since it is easier to use in proofs. However, for our purposes, it is harder for wander to reason about, because to conclude a Texan triple proof we must apply its continuation at the end. Doing so automatically may not be possible if the continuation’s conclusion and the goal differ syntactically. In particular, this kind of reasoning does not follow the execute the goal strategy that wander implements, since it requires external information about the type of goal we want to prove. Knowing that the continuation must be applied tells us that we must at some point establish an equality between the goal and the continuation’s conclusion.

To circumvent this issue, we exploit the equivalence between Hoare triples and Texan triples, since wander is perfectly capable to reason about Hoare triples. The usual Hoare triple encoding does not have this problem of adding a “must apply” local hypothesis in our proof. Therefore, in our normalization pass, we implement a simplification procedure which translates Texan triples into Hoare triples. This is the lemma employed by this procedure.

Listing 17 highlights the difficulty behind the proof of Texan encodings. In the translation, the additional condition ⌜v = p x⌝ appears, which is precisely what ensures that the continuation’s conclusion and the goal will match syntactically.

Notice how there is a condition on the types of expressions for which this transformation is correct. In particular, it does not work if e is a value. To decide whether a given expression is a value or not, the normalizer simply invokes the decide tactic, which will reduce (compute) the left hand side of the equality to see if it evaluates to none. In the case of HeapLang, this check will always succeed as long as the expression in the weakest precondition is headed by a constructor of HeapLang.Exp.

The final component of wander is the hint search procedure. This procedure is overall similar to Diaframe’s but differs in a couple of places. A hint search procedure strategy seeks to answer a query of the form 𝐻⊫∃𝑥⃗,𝑇𝑥⃗ with a theorem stating ∀𝑦⃗,𝐻∗𝐴𝑦⃗⊢𝑀(∃𝑥⃗,𝑇𝑥⃗∗𝐹𝑦⃗𝑥⃗), which corresponds to the format used in Figure 3. However, since hints are only indexed by atoms in their hypothesis, in the case where 𝐻 is not an atom wander will inspect its shape and perform subqueries. For instance:

  1. 𝐻1∗𝐻2⊫∃𝑥⃗,𝑇𝑥⃗ triggers 𝐻1⊫∃𝑥⃗,𝑇𝑥⃗ or 𝐻2⊫∃𝑥⃗,𝑇𝑥⃗
  2. ▷𝐻⊫∃𝑥⃗,▷𝑇𝑥⃗ triggers 𝐻⊫∃𝑥⃗,𝑇𝑥⃗
  3. (∀𝑒,𝜑(𝑒))⊫∃𝑥⃗,𝑇𝑥⃗ triggers 𝜑(?𝑒)⊫∃𝑥⃗,𝑇𝑥⃗
  4. 𝐻1−∗𝐻2⊫∃𝑥⃗,𝑇𝑥⃗ triggers 𝐻2⊫∃𝑥⃗,𝑇𝑥⃗
  5. 𝑀𝐻⊫∃𝑥⃗,𝑇𝑥⃗ triggers 𝐻⊫∃𝑥⃗,𝑇𝑥⃗ if 𝑀 is introduceable

Out of all the rules above, rule number 3 warrants some scrutiny. Once the 𝜑(?𝑒)⊫∃𝑥⃗,𝑇𝑥⃗ subquery has been answered, wander is left with a choice. If the subquery required ?𝑒 to be given a concrete value, wander must specialize the hypothesis with this value. Otherwise, the result must generalize over ?𝑒 again, since this will become a new output of the hint.

After the hypothesis has been properly decomposed into atoms, wander will try to find a user rule matching the query, and upon failure, transform the target 𝑇 and try again. These transformations in the target correspond to Diaframe’s right rules, but are not mapped one-to-one. The following are the right-rules implemented in wander.

  1. 𝐻⊫▷∃𝑥⃗,▷𝑇𝑥⃗ triggers 𝐻⊫∃𝑥⃗,𝑇𝑥⃗
  2. 𝐻⊫∃𝑥⃗,𝐖𝐏𝑒 {Φ} triggers 𝐻⊫∃𝑥⃗,𝐖𝐏𝑒′ {𝑣,𝐖𝐏𝐾[𝑒′] {Φ}}, where 𝑒=𝐾[𝑒′] and 𝐾 is the maximal context for which 𝑒′ is not a value.

The second rule is new in wander. In Diaframe, a similar effect can be achieved directly through a user rule, by using typeclass programming to extract the context 𝐾 from the given expression. In wander I opted to include this bind rule directly in the hint search procedure.

There are also two Diaframe hint search rules which are missing, namely those to do with existentials. In Diaframe, they work very much as the left-rule number 3. In wander, however, we delegate this processing to the procedure checking whether a user rule matches the query or not.

To illustrate this difference, let us consider an example. Assume that the current environment has a user provided rule 𝐻∗emp⊢∃𝑦,𝑇 𝑎 𝑦 (𝑐+2)∗emp. Notice how 𝑎 and 𝑐 are not bound in the exists. This is because the rule works for any value of 𝑎 and 𝑐, but the values are not provided by the rule. In this context, the hint search procedure receives a query for 𝐻⊫∃𝑦𝑧,𝑇 0 𝑦 𝑧. The matching logic is able to conclude that the previously shown user rule is compatible with the current query, since the 𝑎 of the user rule can be instantiated to 0, the 𝑦 from the query can be taken to be the 𝑦 from the user rule, and the 𝑧 from the query is assigned to the 𝑐+2 from the user rule. The user rule quantified over 𝑎 and 𝑐, but only 𝑎 was given a value. In this case, the value of 𝑐 will be postponed, so it becomes a new output of the rule. The logic in this whole procedure is captured by the theorem in Listing 18. In the prior example, Xᵣᵤₗₑ corresponds to the type of 𝑦, Xᵣₑₛₜ corresponds to the type of 𝑧, and Xₜ to the combination of both. The value of xᵣ for this theorem would be 𝑐+2.

Some notes on performance. As it stands, it is clear that the bottleneck for wander’s performance is the hint search procedure. This is to be expected, since Diaframe suffered the same issue, and reimplemented their hint search procedure in LTac2, forgoing its signature typeclass programming approach in order to gain more control over the search procedure. As it stands wander performs none of these optimizations, and therefore can be quite slow. However, this does not reflect a limitation of the system or the environment, but more so of the time constraints under which wander was developed. In any case, wander has been architectured in such a modular way that the experience of providing one’s own hint search strategy should be plug and play. In the coming section we go over the finer details of wander’s implementation, but not before taking a detour covering Lean’s metaprogramming APIs and how they have been so far exploited in Iris Lean.

Dispatcher. There is a final system which deserves a mention: the pure sidegoals dispatcher. When wander encounters a pure goal, it will generate a pure side condition. If the Wander.useDischarger option is enabled with set_option Wander.useDischarger true, then wander will additionally try to solve the goal by invoking the dispatcher. This is where the existing automation tools for Lean get their opportunity to shine. The default wander dispatcher tries various tactics to close the goal: it starts with with_reducible rfl to deal with most simple equalities which can be solved without aggressive unfolding, tries trivial if this fails, and finally invokes grind as a last resort.

3.4. Background: Metaprogramming in Lean and Iris Lean

An interesting facet of the Iris project is that it mechanizes a logic in a system that, in itself, implements a logic. The Iris project does not limit itself to providing a formalization, however, but also seeks to provide an interface through which one can interact with said logic. This interface is the Iris Proof Mode, which is accessed through custom tactics such as iintro, iapply and iframe. Interestingly enough, and perhaps naturally, Iris developed this Proof Mode by seeking to extend the interface of the system of mechanization it is formalized in. It is therefore not surprising that one is able to identify certain parallelisms between Iris and its system of mechanization, both in terms of the logic and the interface through which it is accessed.

In terms of the logic, in Lean a proposition is a value of type Prop. In Iris, propositions are values of some type PROP for which there is an instance BIBase PROP. With regards to proofs, since Lean is a type theory, proofs of propositions are values whose type is a proposition, and their constructors and elimination principles correspond to the proof rules they are governed by. In Iris, the introduction and elimination rules are provided explicitly by the BI PROP instance, for the connectives available in BIBase PROP. Since Iris is not a type theory, its proofs are represented directly through the use of the ⊢ relation, whose definition is also found in BIBase PROP.

We argue that this parallelism is also reflected in the metaprogramming interfaces available for both systems. To properly showcase this, we give a small introduction to Lean’s metaprogramming API.

Lean metaprogramming API. A metaprogram is nothing more than a function which interacts with our language at the meta level. In practice, this means that the function is able to access the environment, with all available definitions at some point in our source file, as well as interact and manipulate syntactic objects. Therefore, one of the most important types of any metaprogramming API is that of the abstract syntax tree of our programs. Since Lean is a functional programming language, these programs are all expressions, and the type which represents them is Lean.Expr. In the interest of brevity, in this text we use a mathematical notation to exhibit the Lean.Expr type as an Expr grammar, with a standard construction using de Bruijn indices as bound variables #𝑛, with perhaps the more uncommon native projections 𝑡.𝑛 and native string and number literals. Expr is shown in Figure 5.

This definition corresponds to the shape of expressions that the Lean kernel is able to typecheck. The purpose of most metaprograms dealing with expressions is to construct a final expression that is accepted by the kernel. It should be noted that the Lean.Expr type is in itself untyped. In practice this means that metaprograms can, quite easily, create malformed expressions which will be rejected by the kernel, and it can sometimes be complicated to pinpoint the particular source of the bug.

However, thanks to Lean’s metaprogramming capabilities, the community has been able to address this through a Lean library. Qq is a library that provides two notations q(..) and Q(..) with which users are able to construct expressions in a typed way. Q(α) denotes an expression of type α, and q(t) denotes the expression represented by t. Furthermore, inside the parenthesis of both notations one is able to refer to a local variable x through its antiquotation as $x, but only if x is of some type Q(..). The local variable will be used directly in the final term, instead of its expression. In Table 1 we see some examples of how the q(..) notation works. Q(..) is just a notation for Quoted q(..), which is itself just a wrapper over Lean.Expr which keeps track of the expression’s type.

Using Qq to construct Lean.Expr terms is usually much more convenient than using its constructors directly. However, Qq is not used in Lean’s internal code. One of the reasons for this is performance concerns and control. But another reason is that, once terms become complex enough, there are other abstractions that are used to reason over them which are preferred over inspecting the constructors directly. These have to do with two variants of the Lean.Expr type which we have not yet mentioned. Figure 6 introduces them. These are free variables and metavariables.

Free variables 𝑥 stand for universally quantified variables. We can think of them as bound variables, but whose binder information is not found in the expression itself, but in a separate LocalContext. Free variables are represented by a unique identifier which the LocalContext uses to refer them to their declaration.

Metavariables ?𝑥 are the dual concept to free variables, an existentially quantified variable. Where free variables stand for any value of their type, metavariables are meant to refer to a particular value of that type. They represent a hole in the expression, which must be filled in. Opposite to free variables, metavariables provide a LocalContext in the declaration, the local context under which the value they stand for must be interpreted. Metavariables are also represented by a unique identifier, which the MetavarContext associates with the metavariable’s declaration. This declaration, beyond having read-only information like the type, local context or display name, also records whether the metavariable has been assigned to a value, and if so, the value itself. This optional value field is mutable, but must only be assigned once.

Functions dealing with terms containing free variables or metavariables receive the corresponding LocalContext and MetavarContext through the MetaM monad. As we have stated before, LocalContext is a read-only parameter while MetavarContext is mutable. Most other metaprogramming monads wrap around MetaM, like for instance TacticM which simply adds a mutable list of goals.

The purpose of a tactic script is to construct a term given its type, more specifically a proof term given a proposition. However, to provide an interactive interface with its users, tactics communicate with one another through the concept of goals. A goal is nothing more than a metavariable that has not been assigned yet. Implementing a tactic in Lean is not much more complicated than defining a value TacticM Unit. From within the TacticM monad tactics are able to access the list of goals, assign them, and update the list with the remaining unsolved goals, possibly even adding to the list. When a tactic script is run to fill in a term of type T, a new metavariable of type T is created in the empty context, the tactics in the script are run with this new metavariable as the initial goal, and once run, all metavariables in the original goal are substituted by their assigned values and the resulting term is returned. It is then the responsibility of the kernel to ensure that there are no dangling free variables or metavariables, and that the produced term typechecks correctly.

Metaprogramming in Iris Lean. In Iris Lean we build on top of this API abstractions that allow us to more easily deal with metaprograms manipulating terms in the Iris logic. In this case, the main difference between Lean’s and Iris’ logic is that Iris has an additional spatial context. This spatial context is represented by the proposition in the left-hand side of the ⊢ relation, and can be seen as a ∗-separated list of hypotheses. To allow users to interact with this spatial context with a similar API to the one for LocalContext, we need to record additional information about the hypothesis contained in the spatial context. This extra information is recorded by the ProofMode.Hyps datastructure which presents a structured view over the proposition encoding the spatial environment.

Listing 19 shows a simplified definition of the real Iris.ProofMode.Hyps. This consists of a view of some expression 𝑒 as a (possibly empty) tree of ∗ nodes. The leaves of this tree are the spatial hypotheses as shown in our proof mode, and store information such as the user provided name, and a unique identifier with which they can be referred to. Metaprograms can use this unique identifier to retrieve the hypothesis’ declaration, as well as to request its removal or modification. Differently from the LocalContext, operations which mutate the underlying expression also provide a proof showing that the transformation is correct. For instance, removing hypothesis 𝐻 out of Δ provides a Δ′ and a proof that Δ⊣⊢Δ′∗𝐻. These proofs are needed to properly interleave the spatial contexts in our proofs, usually using transitivity of the ⊣⊢ or ⊢ relations.

Iris Lean tactics live in their own monad, ProofModeM. This monad is nothing more than a thin wrapper around TacticM which holds its own goals field separate from TacticM’s. The purpose of ProofModeM is more to clearly denote which tactics belong to the Iris Proof Mode, and to restrict certain operations to them. For instance, Iris Lean implements its own version of typeclass search which resembles Lean’s implementation but lifts some of the restrictions it imposes, trading performance for flexibility. This typeclass synthesis algorithm is invoked through the ProofModeM.trySynthInstanceQ function, which can only be run under the ProofModeM monad.

However, the parallelisms with Lean’s tactics end here. While Lean tactics have a signature TacticM Unit, tactics in Iris Lean have a different signature: Hyps inst e → (g : Q($prop)) → ProofModeM Q($e ⊢ $g). An Iris Proof Mode tactic is given a spatial context and a goal to derive in it, and is expected to return a proof that the goal holds under the given spatial context. The hypothesis and Iris goal are parsed from the current Lean goal, and the result of the Iris tactic is assigned to it. Since the tactic is run in the ProofModeM monad, it is allowed to generate new goals. However, goals are no longer the preferred method of communication between tactics. Instead, a continuation passing style is preferred. Consider as an example the implementation of iloeb, whose logic is implemented by iLoebCore in Listing 20.

The iLoebCore function is a good example of what an Iris Lean tactic looks like. The signature fits almost precisely what we mentioned before, excluding some tactic-specific arguments such as IH and targets. Internally, iLoebCore makes use of the functions used internally by other tactics, such as iIntroCore for the iintro implementation or iModIntroCore for the implementation of imodintro. We observe that the way these functions are composed is by passing in continuations. iRevertIntro is a particularly convoluted example. Observe how its continuation receives another continuation k, which itself expects another continuation as well. In this case, the continuation used is addBIGoal, which can be seen as the identity tactic in ProofModeM, since its implementation simply adds a goal to be solved later and returns the metavariable as its proof.

However, there are a couple of limitations to this approach. First, notice how, even though we have a separate goals field in our ProofModeM monad, after our Iris Lean tactic runs, the extra goals are passed to the TacticM monad’s state. In particular, the state maintained by ProofModeM is only kept as long as the tactic is running, afterwards all remaining obligations are added to the TacticM state, and the next goal will need to parse the spatial context from the type of the next goal again. Secondly, since goals generated in the ProofModeM monad are not meant to be accessed by other ProofModeM tactics, composition is restricted to a continuation-passing style. This is a bit inconvenient, since Lean has excellent support for monadic computations, and some of its features are lost in the continuation-passing style. For example, one is no longer able to do early returns from within a continuation. Another example is the syntax for inserting tracing nodes, which themselves use a continuation to designate a section of code. These sections are used by the profiler to define sampling points, and by the tracing system to group together traces associated by a logical operation. However, these trace nodes are not able to capture correctly disjoint sections of code if these are receiving the rest of the program as a continuation, because their execution only ends when the execution of the whole program does.

Nevertheless, none of these limitations are fundamental to Iris Lean. In the next section, we show how they can be circumvented by changing some of these definitions.

3.5. Metaprogramming in Wander

The WanderM monad. For wander’s development, I wanted to have an API closer to what Lean offers. We have seen in Section 3.4 that this was the case up until the introduction of the ProofModeM monad. The reason why tactics in the ProofModeM monad have the shown signature is that their types depend on a variety of values that live in the context. If we observe the signature of iLoebCore in Listing 20, the function requires a multitude of implicit parameters. The most relevant ones to our concerns are the prop : Q(Type u) and bi : Q(BI $prop) parameters. It is evident to see why prop is required, since it gives the type of Iris propositions for this particular goal, and therefore appears in the type of all of our propositions, but the relevance of bi is less obvious. From looking at the body of iLoebCore, its only usage appears to be in the Hyps type, but looking at the definition of Hyps in Listing 19, it also does not seem to be required anywhere. However, if it had truly not been required, the linter for unused variables in Lean would have reported so. The reason bi is required is that it holds the implementation of emp, ∗, ⊢ and all other connectives associated with the current prop type. Since we have been writing these terms with Qq, it does not appear syntactically in our programs, but the resulting expressions contain it.

Qq is the reason why we need these arguments in the context, and it is also the reason why we cannot hide them in a monad. Not only is it required by most of the types in our context, it is also required that all of these types in our context refer to the definitionally equal instances of these arguments. Therefore, our context must be parameterized by them. For our ease of use, we group all of these parameters inside of a couple of structures, shown in Listing 21.

Observe how BIProp extends BIBaseProp. This is because in some instances, requiring our type of propositions prop to know its BI instance is too strong of a requirement. For instance, when dealing with Iris propositions, and not its proofs, the rules found in the BI instance are not necessary. For those situations where the BI instance is required, we use the BIProp structure, which extends BIBaseProp with the BI instance, as well as the assertion that BI.toBIBase on this instance results in the BIBase instance stored in the substructure. This condition is necessary since otherwise Qq would assume them to be distinct, while it is a user error if two such distinct instances were to exist.

With these structures defined, we are now able to provide the following definition, parameterized over our choice of BIProp, which stands for the analogue to metavariables in Lean.

A Goal for a given type of propositions is then a structure which represents a goal of the shape Γ;Δ⊢𝑀 𝑇, and which additionally stores the datastructure of parsed spatial hypotheses3.

With this new representation, we can more closely mimic the Lean signature for tactics. In wander, this is seen in how wander actions have been implemented. A wander action, such as continue or finish as we saw in Section 3.2, is nothing more than a function in the WanderM monad. The WanderM monad is an Iris Lean equivalent to the TacticM monad in plain Lean. It holds a list of remaining goals to be dispatched, plus some additional information for diagnostic purposes. This monad also has a series of read-only fields such as the configuration for the normalizer, or the discharge function to be used by wander. The definition of the monad can be seen in Listing 23.

The WanderM monad enables us to regain some of the conveniences lost in the ProofModeM monad. In particular, goals become again the preferred method of composition of tactics, or “actions” as they are called in wander, and since goals contain the parsed spatial context, it is not necessary to reparse them. More generally, since now actions are all executed under the same monad context, they can share information between them. So far this has not been exploited extensively, due to time constraints, but it is possible to imagine how it would be beneficial for tactics to share between them, for instance, an index of the spatial context. More generally, the inconveniences introduced by the continuation passing style can all be avoided.

Iris terms metaprogramming API. Beyond a convenient way of representing goals, the development of wander also needed to extend the available API to manipulate Iris propositions and proofs. For the most part, Qq was able to deal with the brunt of the work. However, whenever it is not possible to express some operation with Qq, the existing APIs ended up being woefully inconvenient. One such common case where Qq did not work was when dealing with binders. The idiomatic way to deal with binders in Lean is to use APIs such as lambdaTelescope or mkLambdaFVars which rely on free variables and declarations in the local context to conveniently deal with a dynamic number of binders. Listing 24 contains an example of the usage of these APIs.

In Iris, however, we do not use the same ∀ and ∃ connectives as the host logic, but instead rely on the implementations provided by the BIBase typeclass. Therefore, in wander we implemented an equivalent API, parameterized by a BIBaseProp argument, which would work for the Iris ∀ and ∃ statements.

The situation is unfortunately not as straightforward when dealing with proofs. Because Iris is not a type theory, proofs are not themselves terms, but derivation trees. In particular this means that we must deal explicitly with the spatial context in our transformations, and requires that we make extensive use of transitivity of the ⊢ relation when constructing these proofs. What is needed to deal with binders in proofs is to be able to apply their introduction and elimination principles on a dynamic number of binders. This is achieved by wander’s API through the use of functions mimicking the mkBinderFVars APIs, but which additionally take into consideration the direction of the proof that needs to be generated.

Proving theorems for variable numbers binders. Recall the definition of biabduction rules shown in Figure 3 in Section 3.2.

The biabduction rule format admits a variable number of binders, both in the ∀ in the output and in the ∃ in the input. When wander makes progress by using a rule, it must prove that the transformation it performs is correct. Therefore, this proof must somehow deal with the fact that rules have a dynamic number of binders.

With the APIs we have described so far, this proof could be constructed dynamically by the metaprogram. However, the API to do this would both not be very convenient, nor very efficient or easy to change. Ideally, we would like to prove once that the biabduction rule transformation is correct, and instantiate this theorem whenever needed. This is precisely what wander does, and it states the theorem of rule application in the following way.

This theorem is stated for a single binder for both the ∀ and the ∃. The reason wander is able to use this theorem for any number of variables is that the biabd attribute, for every biabduction rule, produces an auxiliary declaration in which both binders are curried. So, in fact, all rules wander sees do have the above shape. Then, to instantiate the theorem, wander simply transforms the goal into a curried version, applies the theorem, and uncurries the continuation.

To properly support currying of binders in Lean we needed to extend the existing metaprogramming functions to create and manipulate dependent tuples in Lean. To do so, we chose to mimic the existing non-dependent tuples API which lives under the PProdN namespace, to develop a new API, under the PSigmaN namespace. This API implements, among other things, packing and unpacking procedures for ∀ and ∃ binders in the Iris logic, as shown in Listing 27.

To note is how Diaframe chose to deal with this same issue. More generally, in Iris the problem of manipulating variable numbers of binders is addressed through the use of telescopes. Telescopes are an object-level encoding of variable number of binders. In wander, we opted to use currying instead. The benefit of our approach is that it’s simpler, and it does not need any new definitions. On the other hand, Telescopes being an object-level encoding means that operations manipulating them can be proven correct at the object level. Furthermore, the telescopes encoding is definitionally equal to the binders they represent, so there is no need to provide separate functions stating the correctness of the translation like Listing 27 does. Out of these two advantages, the latter is probably the most relevant, since neither wander nor Diaframe require complex reasoning about binders.

4. Other contributions

During my internship I made some contributions to the Iris Lean development that are not explicitly stated in this report. At the time of the start of my internship, the Iris Lean project was not yet at a stage where one could prove properties about programs with it. Not only had HeapLang not been defined, but the 𝐖𝐏 definition was also missing. The Iris Proof Mode was surprisingly well developed, but there were still some common tactics missing. In this context, much of my internship consisted in aiding the project to integrate the necessary components so that I could build upon them to develop wander. These contributions include:

Plainly lemmas. At the beginning of my internship, I implemented a variety of lemmas dealing with the Iris plainly modality as a way of getting accustomed to the codebase and upstreaming process.

Language interface. I ported the language interface found in Iris Rocq. The port also included a change in how the interface is defined, which now makes use of typeclasses instead of canonical structures. The reason Rocq uses canonical structures for this instance, instead of typeclasses, is performance issues that arise from them. Lean’s typeclasses make use of a more restrictive algorithm which allows for more aggressive caching, so generally typeclass synthesis performance is not an issue. Beyond the language interface itself, I also ported the definition and notation of 𝐖𝐏 that builds on top of it, as well as the rules that govern its use. In total this resulted in new files Language.lean, ECtxLanguage.lean, ECtxItemLanguage.lean, WeakestPre.lean, Lifting.lean and ECtxLifting.lean.

Various tactics. I implemented the iloeb, wp_pures and wp_bind tactics. wp_pures and wp_bind in particular required me to reflect HeapLang expressions to extract their evaluation contexts, in contrast with Rocq’s match backtracking approach.

Various case studies. I implemented the LazyCoin.lean example from Iris’ repository, as well as the ClairvoyantCoin.lean and ListFunctions.lean case studies found in Diaframe’s repository.
